cards.front: Recall a key point about Types of Families & Households
cards.back: Nuclear family: two generations (parents and children) living together. Murdock argued the nuclear family is universal and performs four essential functions: sexual, reproductive, economic and educational. Parsons called it the 'isolated nuclear family' - geographically and socially mobile for modern industrial society.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Types of Families & Households
cards.back: Extended family: three or more generations living together or nearby. Vertical extended: grandparents, parents, children. Horizontal extended: aunts, uncles, cousins. Common in pre-industrial and many non-Western societies; declining in the UK due to geographical mobility.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Types of Families & Households
cards.back: Reconstituted/step families: formed when adults with children from previous relationships form new partnerships. About 10% of UK families. Challenges: divided loyalties, relationships with absent parent, new family roles and boundaries.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Types of Families & Households
cards.back: Lone-parent families: one parent living with children. About 25% of UK families with children. 90% headed by women. Causes: divorce, separation, choice. Murray (New Right) argues lone parenthood creates welfare dependency; feminists argue it reflects women's increasing independence.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Types of Families & Households
cards.back: Same-sex families: couples of the same sex, with or without children. Increasingly recognised since civil partnerships (2005) and same-sex marriage (2014). Weeks argues same-sex families create 'families of choice' based on commitment rather than biology. Family diversity is now the norm rather than the exception.

cards.front: What should you know about sociology exam tips?
cards.back: When discussing family types, always: define each type clearly, use statistics (25% lone-parent, 10% step), name specific sociologists (Murdock, Parsons, Weeks), and evaluate whether the nuclear family is still the 'norm' or just one type among many.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: The nuclear family is the normal and best type of family for all societies. Correct: While the nuclear family has been the most common type in the UK, family diversity is now the norm: 25% of families with children are lone-parent, cohabitation has increased, same-sex families are legally recognised, and many people choose to live alone.
